business_problem: UC Davis researchers needed a practical way to create convincing materials for scientific datasets under multiple lighting conditions, while also overcoming the long runtimes and memory constraints involved in training and refining custom diffusion control models on typical research hardware.
solution_summary: UC Davis VIDI built a prompt-driven generative AI pipeline for scientific visualization that combines Stable Diffusion with a custom-trained ControlNet model to author materials and textures for rendering. The workflow ingests text prompts, sphere map examples, lighting-direction controls, and training grids rendered from multiple material models with spot lighting at varied orientations. Stable Diffusion provides the pretrained visual prior, while the custom ControlNet enforces pixel-level lighting-direction constraints so the system can generate coherent sphere-map grids under predefined illumination. Training and inference run on Intel Data Center GPU Max Series hardware, accelerated with Intel Extension for PyTorch. Intel oneAPI Base Toolkit is used to optimize workloads across heterogeneous compute, and Intel Tiber AI Cloud supplies scalable cloud resources so the pipeline can run on systems that would not normally support models of this size. Generated sphere maps are inverted into BRDF-based materials, then used to extract or directly generate textures for downstream scientific rendering workflows.

data_flow: Text prompts, sphere map examples, lighting-direction control images, and rendered training grids are fed into a Stable Diffusion plus custom ControlNet pipeline running on Intel GPUs. The model generates sphere maps under controlled lighting, which are then inverted into BRDF-based materials; textures are either extracted from the sphere maps through re-synthesis or generated directly, and the resulting materials are exported for scientific visualization workflows.
business_outcome: The pipeline enabled UC Davis to synthesize realistic materials for scientific visualization while significantly reducing training and inference time, making rapid iteration on model design and material generation practical in a research setting.
metrics: 6 times faster training and inference speeds compared to using CPU only
generate new material maps in as little as 3.18s (4.24 iterations/s)
CPU inference on a top-of-the-line Intel Xeon Platinum processor (18.98s, 1.36 iterations/s)
architecture_clues: The training set uses grids of images rendered with multiple material models and spot lighting at varying orientations to maximize directional information.
The pipeline generates multiple sphere maps lit from distinct angles and interpolates sparse coverage to form a BRDF-based material.
Cloud-based compute resources were used so the pipeline could run on systems that normally could not support models of this size.
The current implementation exports generated materials to a common format; OSPRay support is planned as a future extension.
